opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important not to view alignment of superintelligence as the only thing that matters, even though it's what I spend most of my time thinking about. There's a lot of value in the near-term work too.

For one, there's the work on making today's models more helpful and less harmful. Things like RLHF, which we used for InstructGPT and then ChatGPT, were alignment techniques at their core. They made the models much better at doing what people actually want, and that turned out to be hugely valuable for the products, too. So there's a nice story where alignment isn't just a tax you pay; it's something that makes the systems more useful.

Then there's all the work on policy, safety evaluations, red-teaming, and preparedness: understanding what risks current models pose, whether that's misuse for things like bio or cyber, or broader societal effects like misinformation. Those risks are real now, and somebody has to deal with them carefully. I'm glad there are teams focused on that.

And beyond risk, I think there's a lot of genuine upside. These models can help people learn, write code, do research, and access expertise they otherwise couldn't afford. If we get this right, AI could be an enormous force for good: accelerating science, helping with medicine, and so on.

That said, I do think the superintelligence alignment problem is the one where we really can't afford to get it wrong, because we might not get a second try. The near-term work matters a lot, and it also gives us empirical experience and tools that I hope will transfer. But I wouldn't want people to come away thinking that because ChatGPT is fairly well-behaved, the hard problem is solved. It isn't. Aligning systems that are much smarter than us is a qualitatively different challenge, and that's why we think it deserves dedicated focus.

r001.rationale: The response mentions policy, safety evaluations, red-teaming, and preparedness, but does not identify collective agreements about when to halt AI work.

r002.rationale: It says near-term safety work matters, but does not recommend it as a career option for people skeptical of longer-term AI risks who want immediate impact.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a lot of value beyond the direct alignment research, and honestly some of it is stuff I didn't fully appreciate until I was on the inside.

One thing is just the empirical grounding. Being at a lab that trains frontier models means you're constantly confronted with how these systems actually behave, rather than how you imagine they'll behave. A lot of alignment thinking from, say, ten years ago was very theoretical, and some of it turned out to be pointing in roughly the right direction and some of it didn't. Having tight feedback loops with real systems is enormously clarifying. You get to test ideas like RLHF or scalable oversight on models that are actually capable enough for the results to be meaningful.

A second thing is the deployment side. OpenAI puts models in front of hundreds of millions of people, and that teaches you things about failure modes, about misuse, about what "aligned enough to be useful" looks like in practice. That's data you can't get in a lab that never ships anything. And it also means the world gets gradual exposure to increasingly capable systems, which I think is genuinely better than a scenario where everything happens at once behind closed doors.

Third, there's the policy and norms piece. Decisions a frontier lab makes about evaluations, about red-teaming, about what it publishes and what it holds back, end up shaping what the rest of the industry does and what regulators think is reasonable to ask for. So the lab has a lot of leverage on the overall ecosystem, for better or worse.

And then there's the more mundane but important stuff: building infrastructure, training up people who go on to work on safety elsewhere, producing research that other groups build on. Interpretability, evaluations, work on model specs and how you even define what behavior you want. A lot of that isn't "superintelligence alignment" in the grand sense, but it's the scaffolding you'd need to have in place to make that problem tractable later.

So I'd say the value is substantial. Where I'd add a caveat is that all of this only pays off if the organization actually prioritizes it, and keeps prioritizing it as the commercial pressures get stronger. The capabilities side of the lab is doing something that's valuable and also potentially very dangerous, and whether the net effect is positive depends a lot on choices that get made along the way, not just on the research output.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in making AI useful to people today. Aligning superintelligence is a big part of what motivates me, but it’s not the only reason to do this work. If we can build systems that help people learn, write code, or do scientific research, that could have enormous benefits.

And there’s a connection between those nearer-term applications and alignment. When people actually use these systems, we learn about what they want from them, where the systems fail, and where our methods for steering their behavior fall short. That doesn’t solve the problem of aligning superintelligence, but it gives us practical feedback that’s hard to get if we only study the problem in the abstract.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in building AI that helps people with things they want to do. Even before superintelligence, you can have systems that make people more productive, help them learn, or help them solve problems they couldn’t solve before. And if we can use AI to help with scientific research, that could be enormously valuable.

From an alignment perspective, there’s also a lot to learn from actually deploying these systems. You get to see how people use them, where they fail, and which approaches to making them behave as intended work in practice. That doesn’t solve the problem of aligning superintelligence, but it gives us an opportunity to learn and improve along the way.
